title: Sun Simiao on the Great Physician

confidence.note: The book survives and is conventionally dated 652; the historian Yan Liu dates it more cautiously to the 650s. Sun's birth year is uncertain (581 is given with a question mark), but the ethical teaching in the text is not in doubt.

summary: A 7th-century Chinese formulary sets out what a great physician must know and be: deeply read, compassionate to all, aware that a life is worth more than gold.
body: In the 650s the Tang physician Sun Simiao, who had taught himself medicine after a sickly youth, completed *Essential Formulas Worth a Thousand in Gold for Emergencies* (*Beiji qianjin yaofang*), thirty scrolls of remedies chosen so that help could be found fast in a crisis. He also laid down what a great physician must be. The reading list ran from the medical classics to history, Laozi and even divination, and the doctor was bound by rules of conduct: treat every patient with compassion, whatever their rank. The title carried the point. Human life, he wrote, is more precious than a thousand pieces of gold.

links.note: Another founding statement of a physician's duties, from a different tradition.
Sun's later Supplement copied drug descriptions from the state materia medica.

title: China's first state pharmacopoeia

confidence.note: The completion in early 659 is well recorded and a copy dated 731 survives in Japan. Sources differ on details (22 or 23 compilers, 54 or 55 scrolls), and a Chinese government site calls it the world's first pharmacopoeia, whereas the scholarly sources consulted claim priority only within China.

people: Su Jing (fl. 657), official who proposed the revision
summary: In 659 the Tang court issued a revised, illustrated drug book for the whole empire. Within ten years a copy had reached Dunhuang; by 731 another was in Japan.
body: In 657 the official Su Jing told Emperor Gaozong that the standard drug book, compiled by Tao Hongjing a century and a half earlier, was riddled with errors. Twenty-two officials, twelve of them court medical specialists, gathered medicines from across the empire, and early in 659 they delivered the *Newly Revised Materia Medica* (*Xinxiu bencao*): about 850 substances, 114 of them new, with fresh descriptions and illustrations. It was the first materia medica sponsored by a Chinese government, and the state pushed it outward. Prefectural teachers of medicine used it as a guidebook, a copy reached Dunhuang by 669, and another survives in Japan dated 731.

links.note: It revised Tao Hongjing's annotated edition of the Divine Farmer's classic.
Li Shizhen's compendium, nine centuries later, reorganized the same tradition.

title: The bronze acupuncture man

confidence.note: A university museum dates the figure to 1027 (the fifth year of the Tiansheng era); another account places it only within the Tiansheng reign, 1023–1031. The wax-and-water examination is told as fact in museum and government accounts, but none of the sources consulted cites a Song-period description of it.

people: Wang Weiyi, Song court medical officer
summary: In 1027 a Song medical officer cast a life-sized bronze man studded with 657 named acupuncture points, a teaching model and a national standard.
body: In 1027 the Song court medical officer Wang Weiyi produced a life-sized bronze human figure, about 170 centimeters tall, with 657 acupuncture points carved into its surface, each about 1.2 centimeters deep and labeled with its name. A university museum calls it the first national standard for where the points lay. Wang's *Illustrated Manual of Acupoints on the Bronze Man* was reprinted in 1443. Accounts say the figure doubled as an exam: coated in wax and filled with water, it let liquid out only when a student's needle found the right point. By the Ming Zhengtong period the points had become unrecognizable, and a new figure was cast.

links.note: Rules in Wang's manual go back to the Inner Classic.

title: Song Ci and forensic medicine

confidence.note: Most sources date the book to 1247, though one scholarly editorial says 1248; its content and later spread are well attested. The claim to be the earliest such book comes from Chinese government and review sources and has not been tested here against earlier texts. The famous case of flies gathering on a murderer's sickle is omitted because no source opened here confirmed its wording.

people: Song Ci (1186–1249), judicial official and author
summary: A 13th-century Chinese judge wrote a systematic handbook for examining bodies, long treated as the earliest of its kind: hanging versus strangling, suicide versus murder.
body: In 1247 Song Ci, a Southern Song official from Fujian who had four times served as a senior judge in criminal courts, completed *Collected Writings on the Washing Away of Wrongs* (*Xiyuan jilu*), a systematic guide to examining bodies in suspicious deaths ranked in Chinese accounts as the earliest of its kind. Drawing on his cases, it covered inquest law, the changes a corpse goes through, and how to tell hanging from strangulation, suicide from murder, and wounds made before death from those made after. It even noted how lividity could show that a body had been moved. Dozens of later Chinese manuals followed it, and it spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

title: Variolation in China

date.display: by the mid-16th century (earliest clear text 1549)

traditional.note: An oral tradition credits a Taoist or Buddhist monk or nun with inventing inoculation around 1000 CE, though Joseph Needham found no firmer evidence than that it was widely accepted.

confidence.note: Wan Quan's treatise of 1549 is the earliest clear written reference usually cited; a 2026 review of Chinese sources places the practice's establishment in Jiangxi somewhere between 1465 and 1572. Stories placing its invention in the Tang or Song dynasties lack corroboration. The earliest detailed records known are Chinese, but where and when variolation began is still uncertain.

people: Wan Quan, 16th-century Ming physician, author of *Douzhen xinfa*
Kangxi Emperor (reigned 1662–1722), smallpox survivor who had his children inoculated
summary: Ming doctors gave children a mild dose of smallpox, often blown up the nose as powdered scab, well over a century before inoculation reached Europe.
body: Long before Europe heard of it, healers in China were deliberately giving children a mild case of smallpox to spare them a deadly one. The earliest clear written mention usually cited is in Wan Quan's *Douzhen xinfa*, a treatise on pox diseases published in 1549. Records then place inoculators in Jiangxi and in Taiping County, Anhui, during the Longqing reign (1567–1572), and a 2026 review concludes that the practice took hold in Jiangxi between 1465 and 1572 before spreading through the Yangtze basin.

Chinese texts describe four methods: dressing a child in a sufferer's clothes; plugging a nostril with cotton soaked in pustule fluid; inserting a damp pellet of ground scab; or blowing dried scab powder into the nose through a silver or bamboo tube. Inoculators chose donors with mild cases and refined their material by repeated passage to lower the risk. Under the Qing the practice won imperial backing. The Kangxi Emperor, himself a smallpox survivor, had his own children inoculated and sent inoculators from Jiangxi to Mongolia.

myth.tradition: Inoculation was invented around 1000 CE, by a physician of Mount Emei who treated the son of a Song prime minister, or by a Taoist or Buddhist monk or nun.
myth.record: The Mount Emei and Tang-era origin stories appear in Qing-dynasty texts written centuries later and lack independent corroboration; the monk-or-nun version is an oral tradition for which Needham found no firm evidence. Well-attested evidence begins in the 16th century.

links.note: India's inoculation tradition, documented mainly from the 18th century.

title: Li Shizhen's Compendium of Materia Medica

confidence.note: Completion in 1578 is agreed. The first printing is dated 1590 (Wellcome Collection, for the Nanjing engraving), 1593 (Paul Unschuld) and 1596 (a 2026 study, which calls it posthumous). The differences may reflect the start of engraving, its completion and later circulation, but the sources consulted do not reconcile them.

place: Qizhou (in modern Hubei) and Nanjing, Ming China
people: Hu Chenglong, Nanjing publisher of the first edition
summary: One physician spent 27 years on a drug encyclopedia of 1,892 substances, from waters and minerals to the human body, with 11,096 prescriptions.
body: Li Shizhen (1518–1593), born into a family of physicians in Qizhou, in what is now Hubei, spent 27 years reading, collecting and checking before he finished the *Bencao gangmu* (*Compendium of Materia Medica*) in 1578, at the age of 60. It crowned some 1,600 years of Chinese writing on drugs, but Li broke with the habit of piling new notes on old ones. He gave each substance one correct name as its heading, sorted what was known under up to ten standard subheadings, and flagged his predecessors' errors.

The result described 1,892 substances, ordered from waters, fires, soils and metals through plants and animals up to the human body, with 11,096 prescriptions and 1,109 illustrations in roughly 1.6 to 2 million characters. The first edition was engraved at Nanjing by Hu Chenglong in 1590 and Li died in 1593; one recent study calls the book posthumous, and sources date its publication anywhere from 1590 to 1596. Modern scholars admire its systematic classification, though one recent study stresses that its parallels with Linnaeus are functional, not formal.

links.note: The culmination of the tradition that began with the Divine Farmer's classic.

title: The Donguibogam

confidence.note: Copies of the 1613 government printing survive and are designated National Treasures in South Korea; the stages of compilation (ordered 1596, completed 1610) are recorded in Korean historical sources summarized by the Korea Institute of Oriental Medicine.

people: Heo Jun (1539–1615), royal physician and compiler
King Seonjo of Joseon (died 1608), who ordered the work
summary: Ordered by a king after a war and finished in exile, a Korean royal physician's medical encyclopedia was reprinted across East Asia for centuries.
body: In 1596 King Seonjo of Joseon ordered his physician Heo Jun to compile a new medical encyclopedia; Heo had won the king's trust escorting him north during the Japanese invasion of 1592. When Seonjo died in 1608, Heo took responsibility and was exiled, and he used the exile to finish the book in 1610. Printed by the government in 1613, the *Donguibogam* (*Treasured Mirror of Eastern Medicine*) drew on about 180 earlier works and was republished dozens of times in China, Japan and Vietnam. UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World Register in 2009, citing its ideal of state-led preventive medicine and public health.
